summary: Most nationalities buy a US$30 tourist visa on arrival, good for 30 days and extendable once, while citizens of the EU (except Ireland) and the other Schengen states enter visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180 under the EU agreement and citizens of Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand visa-free for 30 days. The Migration Service says the visa on arrival is issued at every official border post, including land crossings from Indonesia.

travelInsurance.text: No official source states a travel insurance requirement for entry to Timor-Leste; the Migration Service's entry conditions and visa documents do not include it. It is strongly advisable, with medical-evacuation cover — hospitals are basic and serious cases are evacuated to Darwin or Singapore.

source.name: Migration Service of Timor-Leste — Tourist Visa

onwardTicket.text: Not systematically checked, but airlines and border officers may ask for evidence of onward travel. Carry your return booking.

source.name: Migration Service of Timor-Leste — Tourist Visa

proofOfFunds.text: Every visitor must have access to funds sufficient for the stay and may be asked to show them. For tourist, transit and business (Class 1) visa holders not sponsored by family or another contact in the country, the law sets US$100 per entry plus US$50 per day of stay.

source.name: Migration Service of Timor-Leste — At the Border (entry conditions, traveller declaration)

declarations.name: Arrival and departure declaration (Customs Trade Single Window)
declarations.text: All travellers must complete an official declaration online before arrival and before departure. One form serves Migration, Customs, quarantine, the Ministry of Health and the Central Bank. Keep the QR code or PDF to show border officials.

source.name: Migration Service of Timor-Leste — At the Border (entry conditions, traveller declaration)

currencyLimits.text: If you plan to bring cash or travellers cheques worth USD 20,000 or more, you must get authorisation from the Central Bank of Timor-Leste before you arrive. The online arrival and departure declaration that every traveller submits also serves the Central Bank as well as customs.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — Timor-Leste travel advice: entry requirements

notes: Duty-free allowances are modest (roughly 200 cigarettes and a small quantity of alcohol per adult). Declare anything beyond personal use.

payments.text: Timor-Leste uses the US dollar. Cards are accepted only at a few hotels and supermarkets in Dili, and ATMs are scarce and unreliable outside the capital. Bring clean, small-denomination dollar notes, as change for large bills is hard to find.

safety.text: Australia advises a high degree of caution in Timor-Leste because of crime and limited healthcare. Street-gang fighting and political demonstrations occur and minor disputes can turn violent, so avoid protests and large gatherings. Many taxis are unsafe, roads flood in the wet season, and crocodile attacks are reported in the east and along the south coast, with sightings on beaches in Dili.

bestTimeToVisit.text: The May–October dry season brings the best roads, trekking and world-class diving around Atauro Island; the wet season (roughly November–April) can cut off rural roads.

tips.text: Have US$30 in cash ready for the visa on arrival. Cards are not accepted, ATMs and currency exchange may not be available at the border, and small bills are easier for any change.

Crossing overland from Indonesian West Timor (Batugade/Motaain)? The Migration Service says the visa on arrival is issued at land posts too, but Australia's advice still says to get a visa first. Confirm with the Migration Service or the consulate in Kupang before you travel.
Outside Dili, roads are rough and public transport minimal. Hire a 4WD (ideally with driver) for mountain districts, and allow far more time than distances suggest.
Malaria and dengue occur year-round. Use repellent and consider prophylaxis for rural stays. Bring any medication you need; pharmacies outside Dili are very limited.
Atauro Island, a short boat ride from Dili, sits on some of the world's most biodiverse reefs — dry-season visibility is superb, and community homestays make an easy overnight trip.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for Timor-Leste?
faq.answer: Most nationalities do not need anything in advance: a US$30 tourist visa on arrival, valid 30 days, is issued at official border posts. Citizens of the EU and the other Schengen states are visa-free for up to 90 days in any 180-day period under the EU–Timor-Leste agreement (Ireland and the UK are not covered), and citizens of Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand are visa-free for 30 days.

faq.question: What do I need for the visa on arrival?
faq.answer: A passport valid for at least 6 months on the date of entry, US$30 in cash, and the completed online arrival declaration. Officers may also ask for evidence of funds, accommodation and an onward or return booking.

faq.question: Can I extend my stay in Timor-Leste?
faq.answer: Yes, once. Apply in person at the Migration Service headquarters in Dili, ideally at least 15 days before your visa expires. A tourist visa can normally be extended once only, for a further 30 days, for a US$40 fee; processing takes up to 15 days.

faq.question: What currency does Timor-Leste use?
faq.answer: The US dollar is the official currency (with local centavo coins). Bring cash. Cards work only in a few Dili establishments, and ATMs are unreliable. Small, clean bills are the most practical.

faq.question: Can I cross overland from Indonesia to Timor-Leste?
faq.answer: Yes, via the Batugade/Motaain crossing from West Timor. The Migration Service says the tourist visa on arrival is available at all official border posts, including land crossings, and the UK Foreign Office says you can buy one at Batugade. Australia's advice still says land arrivals need a visa before arrival, so confirm with the Migration Service or the Timorese consulate in Kupang before you cross.
